prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: This, Filling, Blue

outputs.L1:
This is where you leave me.  
Filling of old salt and ponderous,  
what’s left of your voice in the air.  
Blue honeycreeper thrashed out  
to a ragged wind, whole months  
spent crawling this white beach  
raked like a thumb, shucking, swallowing  
the sea’s benediction, pearled oxides.  

Out here I am the body invented naked,  
woman emerging from cold seas, herself  
the raw eel-froth met beneath her tangles,  
who must believe with all her puckering  
holes. What wounds the Poinciana slits  
forth, what must turn red eventually.  
The talon-mouths undressing. The cling-cling  
bird scratching its one message; the arm  
you broke reset and broke again. Caribbean.  

Sky a wound I am licking, until I am drawn new  
as a lamb, helpless in the chicken wire of my sex.  
I let every stranger in. Watch men change faces  
with the run-down sun, count fires  
in the loom-holes of their pickups, lines of rot,  
studying their scarred window-plagues,  
nightshade my own throat closed tight  
against a hard hand.  

Then all comes mute  
in my glittering eye. All is knocked back,  
slick hem-suck of the dark surf, ceramic  
tiles approaching, the blur of a beard.  
The white tusk of his ocean goring me.  
This world unforgiving in its boundaries.  
The day’s owl and its omen  
slipping a bright hook  
into my cheek—
outputs.L2:
Here is the place where you abandon me.  
Heavy with ancient salt, thick and burdened,  
the last trace of your voice hangs in the air.  
A blue honeycreeper beats itself against  
a torn, unruly wind; entire months  
have been spent dragging myself across this pale shore,  
combed smooth like the pad of a thumb,  
opening shells, taking in  
the ocean’s blessing, its pearl-like rusts.  

Here, I become a body imagined without covering:  
a woman rising from icy water,  
herself the raw foam of eels caught in her knotted hair,  
forced to trust with every tightened opening.  
Whatever injures the Poinciana cuts outward;  
whatever must redden will do so in time.  
Claw-shaped mouths strip things bare.  
The cling-cling bird scrapes out its single warning;  
the arm you shattered is set, then shattered once more.  

Caribbean.  
The sky is an injury I keep tasting  
until I am made over, new as a lamb,  
powerless inside the wire mesh of my own womanhood.  
I admit every unknown man.  
I watch their faces alter with the failing sun,  
count flames in the woven gaps of their pickup beds,  
the streaks of decay,  
examining their scarred, diseased-looking windows,  
while nightshade seals my throat  
against the pressure of a brutal hand.  

Then everything falls silent  
inside my shining eye.  
Everything is driven backward:  
the wet, sucking edge of black surf,  
ceramic tiles moving nearer,  
the indistinct shape of a beard.  
His ocean’s white tusk pierces me.  
This world has no mercy in the borders it draws.  
The owl of daylight, carrying its signs,  
slides a bright hook  
into my cheek—
outputs.L3:
The poem presents a speaker abandoned in a coastal Caribbean landscape, where the absence of someone who has left continues to haunt everything around her. The setting is not simply a backdrop but an active, oppressive presence: the sea, the shore, the heat, and the surrounding natural world all seem to intensify the speaker’s loneliness and vulnerability. Although the person is gone, their presence lingers in memory and sensation, shaping the speaker’s experience of the landscape as a place of loss.

Throughout the poem, the speaker’s body is portrayed as exposed, wounded, and transformed by desire, violence, and the sea. Her physical self seems inseparable from the environment around her, as though the elements have marked and reshaped her. Desire is not presented as gentle or comforting; instead, it appears connected to injury, invasion, and suffering. The sea, often associated with beauty or freedom, becomes part of this process of erosion and exposure, emphasizing how vulnerable the speaker feels.

The poem’s recurring images of birds, wounds, and red blossoms deepen this atmosphere of danger. Birds may suggest omens or restless movement, while wounds point directly to pain and bodily harm. The red blossoms, though beautiful, also evoke blood and injury, creating a disturbing link between natural beauty and violence. These images suggest that harm is not accidental but inevitable, woven into the world the speaker inhabits.

The speaker’s encounters with strange men are presented as threatening and dehumanizing. These men appear not as individuals offering connection, but as figures of fear, danger, and physical power. Their presence emphasizes the speaker’s vulnerability and the way her body is exposed to the possibility of violation. The poem captures a sense of being watched, approached, or acted upon, rather than being treated as fully human.

By the end, the poem leaves the reader with a powerful sense of entrapment. The speaker exists in a world that is unforgiving, where memory, desire, nature, and human violence all contribute to her suffering. Even beauty is unstable and dangerous: flowers, birds, and the sea do not offer escape, but instead reinforce the sense that pain is everywhere. The poem ultimately portrays a landscape in which abandonment and vulnerability become inescapable, and where the speaker remains trapped within both her body and her surroundings.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a violent and unsettling vision of abandonment, bodily vulnerability, and sexual violation through the imagery of a Caribbean seascape. Rather than offering the sea as a place of beauty, escape, or renewal, the poem transforms it into a hostile field of exposure. Surf, birds, wounds, flesh, and predatory human figures become part of the same disturbing landscape. The natural world does not soften the speaker’s suffering; instead, it records and intensifies it. The Caribbean setting is rendered through fragmented, surreal images that suggest both physical injury and psychological disorientation, as if trauma has broken the speaker’s perception into sharp, unstable pieces.

Throughout the poem, the body appears not as whole or protected, but as opened, marked, and vulnerable. Images of wounds and flesh emphasize the speaker’s exposure to violence, while the presence of birds and the sea suggests a world that watches, circles, consumes, or erodes. The men in the poem appear predatory, linked to threat and violation rather than intimacy or care. Sexual violence is therefore not presented as a single isolated act, but as something that reshapes the speaker’s relationship to the body, to memory, and to place. The speaker becomes both the site of harm and the witness to it, forced to inhabit a body that has been made painfully visible.

The poem’s fragmented and surreal style mirrors the effects of trauma. Its images do not unfold in a calm or orderly way; they arrive abruptly, like flashes of memory or sensation. This broken form suggests that violation cannot be neatly narrated or contained. Instead, it appears through bodily signs, violent metaphors, and a landscape that seems to bear the pressure of what has happened. The sea, the shore, and the creatures that move through them become a brutal register of damage and survival.

In this way, the poem turns the Caribbean seascape into more than a setting. It becomes an extension of the speaker’s wounded consciousness, a place where beauty and brutality are inseparable. The boundaries between body and landscape, victim and witness, memory and present experience begin to collapse. Yet the poem also insists on boundaries that cannot be forgiven or erased: the boundary of the violated body, the boundary between survival and erasure, and the boundary between witnessing violence and being consumed by it. By the end, the speaker is remade by trauma into exposed, perceiving flesh, while the landscape stands as a harsh testimony to abandonment, violation, endurance, and the refusal to make suffering beautiful.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a visceral, surreal free-verse poem set on a Caribbean beach after a breakup, using dense imagery of sea, birds, wounds, sex, and violence, in a contemporary literary style.
counterfactuals.output:
After you left, the beach kept chewing.

All afternoon the Caribbean  
dragged its blue tongue over the sand,  
over the place where our bodies had been  
a hot, ruined alphabet—  
hips, salt, your mouth  
opening like a knife in the fruit.

The gulls came down with their priest-eyes,  
white robes filthy at the hem,  
and argued over a fish head  
silvering in the sun.  
One lifted a ribbon of gut  
and the wind wrote your name with it.

I walked barefoot through the noon glare,  
past conch shells pink as inner ears,  
past boys with machetes splitting coconuts  
with the clean sound of bones making up their minds.  
The sea grapes trembled.  
The palms clattered their green weapons.

Every wave arrived wearing your hands.  
Every wave left with a little more of me.

I wanted to be beautiful in my suffering,  
but the body is an animal with poor manners.  
It leaks. It hungers. It remembers  
the rough hymn of teeth at the shoulder,  
the bed’s dumb violence,  
the way desire can enter a room  
and overturn every chair.

Now my skin is a torn net.  
Now the sun presses its thumb  
into the bruise of the horizon.  
Pelicans drop from the sky like verdicts,  
stabbing the water, rising  
with nothing or something—  
a flash, a thrash, a life  
still trying to be whole.

I think of your back  
as you walked away:  
dark, wet, final,  
a door the ocean invented  
and shut.

Behind the hotel, hibiscus flowers  
flare red as fresh wounds.  
A crab drags its armored loneliness  
into a hole.  
The reef goes on grinding  
its cathedral of dead mouths  
into sand fine enough  
to fill the hourglass of my chest.

Night comes bruised purple,  
smelling of rum, diesel, rotting mango.  
The beach bars ignite their little hells.  
Music staggers out—  
bass like a heart kicked down a stairwell.  
Couples lean into each other  
with the doomed tenderness of candles.

I sit where the tide can reach me.

Let it.

Let the water climb my calves,  
my thighs, my waist.  
Let it find the rooms  
your leaving opened in me.  
Let it rinse the bed from my blood,  
the salt from my mouth,  
the bird-screech from my thinking.

But the sea is not mercy.  
The sea is a blue animal  
feeding on the moon.  
It brings back everything:  
your laugh full of broken glass,  
my name in your throat,  
the last kiss—  
not a kiss, but a fist of heat  
closing around the dark.

Above me, frigatebirds circle,  
black scissors cutting the sky  
into strips of afterlife.

I lie down in the wet sand.  
The stars come out like teeth.

Somewhere under the surf,  
a thousand small creatures  
open and close their wounds,  
open and close their bright, blind mouths,  
as if love were only this:  
the body learning  
how much of itself  
can be taken  
and still be called a shore.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an experimental poem in the voice of a woman abandoned on a tropical island, blending mythic birth-from-the-sea imagery with trauma, desire, and ominous natural symbols.
counterfactuals.output:
I was not born—  
I was **washed up**.

Foam braided itself into my hair,  
salt filled my mouth with its bitter gospel,  
and the sea, enormous mother,  
opened her blue thighs around me.

Out I came:  
not infant, not goddess,  
but a woman with blood under her fingernails  
and a name the tide kept taking back.

The island received me without tenderness.

Palms bent like witnesses.  
Black crabs clicked their little verdicts in the sand.  
At dusk, the fruit bats unfolded—  
dark flowers, dark thoughts—  
and the moon rose bruised above the reef.

You left me here.

Do you hear how the coconuts fall at night?  
Like skulls.  
Like promises.  
Like the knock of someone who will not enter.

I build my bed from leaves and wreckage.  
I drink rain from the hollows of stones.  
I speak to the volcanic rock until it warms  
with the fever of my story.

There are mornings  
when the lagoon lies still as a mirror  
and I see myself emerging again—  
hips slick with brine,  
breasts starred with sand,  
a shell opening where my heart should be.

Inside it:  
the animal sound I made  
when your boat became a white tooth  
on the horizon.

Inside it:  
a pearl grown around a wound.

I want you.  
I want to bite the horizon until it bleeds.  
I want your hands, your throat,  
your apology kneeling in the surf.  
I want to be kissed so hard  
the island forgets it is lonely.

But the jungle teaches another grammar.

Vine over bone.  
Root through rib.  
Orchid blooming from rot.

At night the trees lean close  
and whisper with green tongues:  
stay, stay, stay.

The sea brings gifts—  
a drowned bird,  
a sandal split open like a mouth,  
one red hibiscus floating face-down.

Omens accumulate.

The eel in the tidepool coils into a question.  
The clouds gather in the shape of a fist.  
A storm drags its silver chains across the water.

I am learning to read the weather  
as if it were a body:  
the swollen heat,  
the sudden shiver of leaves,  
the pressure before rupture.

If I was born from the sea,  
then I can be born again from rage.

Look—

I have sharpened the conch.  
I have crowned myself with sea urchin spines.  
My shadow walks before me now,  
long and black and hungry.

When the tide withdraws,  
it reveals the reef’s teeth.

When the moon darkens,  
the mangroves lift their roots  
like hands from a grave.

And I, abandoned,  
salt-made, storm-fed,  
stand at the edge of the surf  
calling your name

until it is no longer a name,

but thunder,

but hunger,

but a wave rising higher  
than any boat can survive.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dark lyric poem beginning with the line “This is where you leave me,” featuring a blue honeycreeper, Poinciana, salt, surf, and a threatening encounter near the ocean.
counterfactuals.output:
This is where you leave me,  
where the Poinciana bleeds its red  
over the road like a warning  
no one alive remembers heeding.

A blue honeycreeper flickers  
through the branches—small, electric ghost—  
then vanishes, as if the sky  
had swallowed its own last thought.

Below us, the surf keeps grinding  
its teeth on the reef.  
Salt lifts from the water  
and finds every wound I have not named.

You stand with your back to the ocean.  
He steps from the shadow of the sea wall,  
knife-bright smile, hands hidden,  
the dusk closing around him like a fist.

No one speaks. Even the waves  
seem to draw away and listen.  
The Poinciana drops one petal, then another,  
little flames going dark in the sand.

I taste salt before blood.  
I taste your leaving before your name.  
The honeycreeper cries once from nowhere—  
blue spark in the throat of night—

and the ocean, vast and merciless,  
keeps coming in.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a raw, image-heavy poem about heartbreak and bodily vulnerability in the Caribbean—make it strange, unsettling, and full of birds, red flowers, men, wounds, and sea imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
**HIBISCUS WITH A BROKEN MOUTH**

In the Caribbean, heartbreak sweats through the walls.  
It comes green-backed, salt-eyed,  
dragging its belly over the tile  
like a fish that forgot the sea  
and learned my name instead.

All morning the frigatebirds circle  
with their black scissors open.  
They cut the sky into warnings.  
They cut the men from my memory  
and drop them back in pieces—  
a shoulder in the breadfruit tree,  
a laugh rusting under the zinc roof,  
a hand still warm inside the hibiscus.

Red flowers everywhere.  
Red as bitten tongues.  
Red as church dresses after rain.  
Red as the wound that keeps practicing  
how to be a door.

The men came smelling of rum, diesel,  
mango skin, iron,  
the sea’s old appetite.  
They put their mouths on me  
like fishermen testing knots.  
They called me sweetheart, stormlight,  
little island,  
then left with their pockets full of my shoreline.

Now my body is a reef at low tide.  
Every soft thing exposed.  
Every bright nerve flickering  
for the gulls.

A pelican lands in the basin  
where I wash my blood from the sheets.  
Its beak is a funeral boat.  
Its eyes are two old priests  
who have forgiven nothing.

I feed it a red flower.  
It swallows the blossom whole  
and shudders like a man  
hearing his own name  
spoken by the dead.

Outside, the sea keeps opening  
and opening—  
blue wound,  
salt mouth,  
mother with all her teeth.  
It licks the pier posts clean.  
It takes the drowned light  
into its throat.

I kneel on the bathroom floor,  
bare knees in the hair and sand,  
and count what is still mine:

one rib of moon,  
one cracked heel,  
one breast aching like weather,  
one heart—  
black mango,  
bird-eaten,  
still hanging.

At dusk the egrets arrive,  
white knives in the cane field.  
They stalk the mud  
as if looking for someone’s lost pulse.  
Behind them, the flamboyant trees  
ignite their red crowns  
and the whole road burns beautifully  
without giving warmth.

I think of the men again.  
Their shadows nailed to rum shops.  
Their throats full of conch shell.  
Their hands like crabs  
climbing in and out of me.  
How they praised my softness  
while sharpening themselves  
against it.

The night opens its wet hibiscus.  
Mosquitoes sing over my ankles.  
A rooster screams from a dark yard  
as if dawn has stabbed him early.

Somewhere, a boy throws stones  
at a mango tree  
until the fruit falls bruised  
and golden  
and ashamed.

Somewhere, a woman rinses a knife  
in seawater  
and the sea accepts it  
like kin.

I lie down with my wounds uncovered.  
Let the geckos watch.  
Let the moths worry the lamp.  
Let the birds come close  
with their terrible little feet.

If love returns,  
it will find me strange.

Not island.  
Not sweetheart.  
Not open boat.

But mangrove-rooted,  
salt-scarred,  
red-flowered at the mouth,  
with a hurricane nesting  
in the cage of my chest—

and every bird in the Caribbean  
beating its wings inside me,  
trying to get out.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem that feels like a fever dream of abandonment on a white beach: lush tropical details, broken bones, strangers, pickup trucks, night surf, and a final image of a hook in the speaker’s cheek.
counterfactuals.output:
The beach was white as a hospital sheet,  
white as a lie left out in the sun,  
and the palms kept fanning the heat  
over my face like strangers saying  
stay awake, stay awake.

Coconuts thudded in the dark green crowns.  
Geckos flickered through the hibiscus.  
Somewhere, a mango split open,  
gold pulp crawling with ants  
like a wound that had learned to glitter.

I had been left there—  
or I had walked there after being left—  
the difference blurred in the fever,  
in the salt, in the bright flies  
stitching the air with their black thread.

My bones were not where I remembered them.  
Rib like a cracked oar.  
Wrist like coral snapped under a careless heel.  
All night the surf dragged itself up the shore  
and fell back gasping.

Pickup trucks came and went  
along the sand road behind the sea grapes,  
their headlights swinging through the palms,  
brief, brutal moons.  
Men leaned out, laughing in a language  
I almost knew from dreams.  
Women in wet dresses smoked by the tailgates.  
No one asked my name.  
No one kept it.

The island breathed rot and sugar—  
banana leaves slick with rain,  
rum spilled on the dashboard,  
diesel, jasmine, fish blood,  
the blue stink of low tide.  
Stars shook above me like fever sparks.  
The moon opened and closed  
its one white eye.

I called for you  
into the black surf,  
but the waves wore your voice  
and would not give it back.  
They brought me instead  
a sandal, a dead eel,  
a child’s red comb,  
a bottle full of sand and no message.

By dawn I had become one of the things  
the beach refused to bury:  
driftwood, shell shard,  
a bird with its neck bent wrong,  
a rumor sleeping in the wrack.

Then the strangers returned.  
Their trucks idled in the pink heat.  
Someone said, poor thing.  
Someone said, leave it.

And when I tried to answer,  
when I opened my mouth  
to prove I was still human,  
I felt the line go tight—  
felt the sea, far out, take hold—  
and there it was, shining,  
caught deep in my cheek:  
a hook, small and silver,  
pulling me toward whatever  
had already abandoned me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
